title: A gathering of water, alive
text:
The rivers of South America as one connected network, each stretch passing its water on to the next until it reaches the sea or an inland ending. Touch a river and light runs from your touch down to the sea while the tributaries that gather there light up. Rest a finger a moment, then draw across many: they all light at once and their water runs together. A drag without the rest turns the globe.

There is no route to finish. Every line has somewhere to go.

sections.title: The boto
sections.text:
The boto, the Amazon river dolphin (Inia geoffrensis), is the largest of the river dolphins. It lives in the rivers of the Amazon and Orinoco basins; the botos of the Araguaia and Tocantins are sometimes counted as a species of their own. Adults, the males most of all, are often pink. Its neck bones are not fused, so it can turn its head, and in the high-water months it swims out among the trees of the flooded forest. It seldom leaps: what breaks the water is usually the top of its head and its back. The IUCN lists it as endangered.

The boto here is drawn, not a sighting: when you are close, one may surface in a large river you have just lit (Strahler order 6 or more, in the Amazon, Orinoco or Tocantins system, east of the Andes). Touch it and it dives.

sections.title: To the sea
sections.text:
The Amazon carries about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the oceans. Fresh, it floats on the salt sea as a plume, which the North Brazil Current carries northwest along the coast of the Guianas toward the Caribbean; for much of the second half of the year the current turns back east north of the equator and takes much of the plume with it, toward Africa.

When the lit water reaches a mouth (the Amazon's, the Tocantins's, the Orinoco's) it runs on along streamlines of this month's mean surface current, measured by drifting buoys: the same currents the globe's sea draws. The way out of each estuary is drawn by hand, and the Amazon's tint is drawn from the currents, not observed; the real plume's reach and colour change from year to year.

sections.title: What the lines are
sections.text:
The connections come from RiverATLAS v1.0, a river network derived from elevation data. Only larger channels are drawn: reaches with at least 500 km² of land upstream, plus their downstream connections. That keeps 218,146 of the 1,620,963 South American reaches, merged here into 18,159 stretches between junctions. The great rivers show from far away, the smaller ones as you come closer. A touch snaps to the nearest line drawn.

The tributaries lit above a touch are the ones retained here, not every stream, and not a surveyed catchment boundary.

sections.title: What is measured
sections.text:
Distances are rounded sums of mapped channel lengths along the network, not straight lines. The first, partial stretch is estimated along its simplified line. Areas are RiverATLAS's land upstream of a stretch's lower end, and at its outlet for a whole system. They are here, in What is lit, rather than at the foot: the lit lines show the rest.

The light shows only which way the water goes. Its speed is invented (it runs about 150 points a second on the screen, and no way down takes more than about eight seconds), and the lines grow heavier only where more of what you lit runs together, not with the water's flow. This is not a simulation of rainfall, travel time, present flow, flood risk or navigability.

sections.title: The limits of a line
sections.text: A branching dataset gives each reach one downstream connection. Real rivers can divide, shift, flood, flow through wetlands, and be changed by people. The Casiquiare, for example, links the Orinoco and Amazon systems; this simplified tree cannot express that connection. An inland ending does not mean an empty landscape.

sections.title: Names
sections.text: These rivers are lived places, with many names and meanings. The few river names here are orientation aids, and the words at the foot name only the systems the lit water drains to: a system's name, such as the Amazon, is given to every stretch that drains to the same outlet. A drainage network cannot stand in for the lives, histories, or knowledge of the people along it.

sections.title: How it was made
sections.text: The study's build selected the larger reaches from the RiverATLAS download, merged chains without a retained tributary, simplified the lines to 0.006° and rounded them to 0.001°, never inventing a connection; its source files' checksums travel with the data. For the globe the lines are simplified further, keeping every link, length and area. The coasts, relief and borders are the globe's own. The ways into the sea and the plume's tint are traced by tools/water/build_alive.py from the globe's own currents.
